title: After the home visit
stem:
You are an F2 doctor working an out-of-hours GP shift. Dr Price, another F2 on the same shift, phones you from her car. She has just been to a home visit where a baby had died unexpectedly, and stayed until the paramedics and police arrived.

She is crying and says she doesn't know how she can do her next visit.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Tell her that difficult cases are part of the job.
options.detailed: Difficult cases are part of the job, but saying so now minimises what she has been through.

options.text: Encourage her to carry on with her visits, as patients are waiting.
options.brief: She may not be safe to work right now.
options.detailed: Patients are waiting, which makes this tempting, but her distress may affect her judgement. The clinical lead can make sure they're seen.

options.text: Listen, and let her talk about what happened.
options.brief: She needs someone to listen first.
options.detailed: This was a deeply distressing experience. Letting her talk, without rushing her, is the most important thing you can do right now.

options.text: Suggest she tells the clinical lead, so her remaining visits can be covered.
options.brief: She may not be fit to continue, and the lead can reallocate visits.
options.detailed: After an experience like this, she may not be able to work safely for the rest of the shift. The clinical lead can arrange cover.

options.text: Offer to take her remaining visits yourself.
options.brief: Kind, but may not be possible with your own workload; the lead should decide.
options.detailed: This is a generous offer, but you have your own calls, and the clinical lead is better placed to reallocate work safely.

options.text: Make sure she knows about support available after traumatic events.
options.brief: Support beyond tonight may help her recover.
options.detailed: Debriefs, staff support services and services such as NHS Practitioner Health can help doctors after traumatic events. Making sure she knows about them is important.

options.text: Ask her for the details of the case.
options.brief: She may want to talk, but questioning her about details isn't the right focus.
options.detailed: Letting her talk is helpful, but asking for details may come across as curiosity, and the case is subject to investigation.

options.text: Suggest she writes a reflection on it when she gets home.
options.brief: Reflection may help later, but not as her immediate support.
options.detailed: Reflection can be valuable, but suggesting it now doesn't address her distress or whether she can continue.

explanation.issue: This tests how you support a colleague after a traumatic event, including whether she is fit to continue working.
explanation.keyDetails: She has just seen a baby who died. She is crying and doubts she can continue. Visits are waiting.
explanation.reasoning: [C] listens, [D] makes sure her work is covered safely, and [F] points her to support. The distractors dismiss her ([A], [H]), keep her working ([B]), take on work the lead should allocate ([E]), or focus on details ([G]).
explanation.competing: [E] is the tempting option because it's generous, but the clinical lead is best placed to reallocate visits safely.

references.title: NHS Practitioner Health
references.note: Confidential support for doctors after traumatic events.
